newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar sinks below 120 yen, dragging down Nikkei.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sinks below 120 yen, dragging down Nikkei.

text.p: A seasonal tide of funds flowing into Japan pushed the dollar briefly below 120 yen on Friday, its lowest level in a month, and swept the Tokyo stock market down with it.
Japanese stocks tumbled in tandem with the dollar as renewed strength in the Japanese currency battered shares in blue-chip exporters such as Sony Corp and Honda Motor .
The key Nikkei market average fell by more than two percent as the exchange-rate factor jolted the market out of the relative calm it has enjoyed in recent sessions.

Dealers attributed the dollar's drop to heavy corporate repatriation of funds ahead of the March 31 fiscal year-end to square books and enhance balance sheets, and the belief that the trend will continue for a while.

The greenback sank as low as 119.95 yen in early afternoon trade after standing at around 121 yen in early morning trade and 120.65 yen in late-New York trade. It later recovered its poise and was trading at around 120.40 yen in mid-afternoon.
The 119.95 figure was the lowest dollar level against the yen since late January.
"Trading is very choppy, but the dollar's continued downward bias signals that there is more demand for yen for seasonal reasons," said a dealer at a European bank.
Dealers said a yen buying spree was not only visible against the U.S. dollar but also against other currencies like the German mark.

Currency traders said comments by Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita that Japan's economy was gradually recovering and gaining strength prompted speculative sales by Japanese banks. A stronger economy would generally mean a greater likelihood of rising interest rates, which would in turn boost the yen.
Speaking at a business luncheon, Matsushita also said that stronger private-sector demand is becoming clearer.

But in a surprise move taken as a sign that the BOJ would maintain its ultra-easy credit stance for the time being, the central bank injected a generous amount of funds into the money market in its daily market operation.
The central bank caught the money market off-guard when it injected 200 billion yen ($1.66 billion), even though banks only needed 100 billion yen ($833 million) to make up a shortfall.
The news encouraged some investors to buy dollars on perceptions that the interest-rate gap between Japan and the United States would stay wide enough to keep overseas investments attractive.
On the stock market, the 225-share Nikkei average closed down 2.44 percent, or 464.56 points, at 18,557.

"Blue chips, even those which had managed to go against the feeble state of the market, have started slipping due to the strength seen in the yen, and that is worsening sentiment," said a broker at one of Japan's "Big Four" brokerages.
A stronger currency can make Japanese products less competitive overseas and squeeze exporters' profits.

The Nikkei suffered a series of big losses earlier this year on banking woes and economic worries, sinking to 17,303 in January, its lowest close so far this year, but it had managed to claw back some ground and hold steady recently. ($1=120 yen)
